chunks.x: g rate and pregnancy rate are based on exposed females (adjusted for sales, transfers and purchases); pounds weaned per exposed female = weaning % x average weaning weight, the key production measure.

chunks.t: B4b. Replacement Heifer Purchase and Bred Heifer Sales Record (J. McGrann, 2019)
chunks.x: Records heifer purchases and bred heifer sales. In the heifer development business "the profit is purchased": the initial heifer value is 60% or more of total cost. Record net income for each sale after marketing costs, by delivery date (holding heifers longer raises cost), noting when forward-priced. Include freight even with your own truck and trailer. Track sales separately for AI-bred, natural-service and mixed heifers (efficient markets should pay more for AI-bred). Market methods: direct, auction, web, video, plus two user-defined. For IRS Schedule F, heifer sales go in Part I line 1a and the purchase cost of heifers for resale in 1b; match purchases to sales by production group even across fiscal years.

chunks.t: B. Replacement Heifers Costs and Return Calculation (J. McGrann, 2018)
chunks.x: Overview of the replacement heifer budgets (natural service, conventional AI, contract breeding service, bred heifers and pairs) with projections and closeouts. The weaned heifer's value (her opportunity cost, what she would have sold for) is the biggest cost, about half of total bred-heifer cost after adjusting for culls. Typically only 75-90% of selected heifers breed; 5-20% are culled open at a discounted feeder price, which raises the cost of the ones that breed. A purchased bred heifer returns her first calf about a year sooner than a saved weaned heifer; it takes at least two years from saving a weaned heifer to her weaning a calf. Breeding cost is under 10% of total heifer cost, so never save on protocol, labor or nutrition if it lowers pregnancy rate; pregnancy rate and weaning rate are everything economically. The gap between open and bred heifer value is the value of one more pregnancy. Price selected weaned heifers at steer value (they are the best heifers). Costs are full costs: cash operating, depreciation, bulls, finance (interest on heifer value and half of operating cost for the period), labor, management and G&A; keep heifers as a separate cost center. Genetics is a low-cost input. Small herds (<200 cows) seldom justify raising their own replacements; terminal-cross herds often do better buying replacements. Definitions: annualized ROI = (net income + interest + target margin) / annualized capital; economic cost adds opportunity cost of owned land and equity; sunk costs (costs already incurred, like the cost of producing a weaned calf) are irrelevant to the retain-or-sell decision; yardage = indirect costs charged per head-day.

chunks.t: C1. Cow-Calf Herd Budget Decision Aid User's Manual (J. McGrann, 2017)
chunks.x: Full cow-calf herd budget: production coefficients and costs, a linked vehicle/machinery/equipment sheet, cattle pricing with price slides, then an income statement, a partial budget to evaluate a practice change, SPA reports, sensitivity tables, and a cow investment (NPV bid price) analysis. Enterprise budget = projection of income and expenses for one enterprise; partial budget = only the items that change (quick way to test a change like selling calves as stockers). Key distinctions: direct (variable) vs indirect (fixed) costs; operating cost = direct + indirect; total unit cost = operating + finance; cash vs non-cash (depreciation, unpaid family labor, interest on equity are real costs); opportunity cost (income from the best alternative use of a resource); short-run vs long-run prices (short decisions use current prices, investments need long-run expectations); economic vs accounting values. Spreading indirect costs over more production lowers cost per unit; replacing labor with machinery trades direct cost for indirect cost and does not guarantee more profit. Sunk costs do not affect short-run decisions: e.g. in a drought, graze a forage only if its gross income exceeds the remaining direct costs. Allocate indirect costs by resource use, by variable cost, or by share of gross income, consistently. A cow is worth the discounted net cash she will earn over her life plus salvage (NPV); economic feasibility (does it pay back?) differs from financial feasibility (how it is financed). Economic principles: add an input while added value exceeds added cost; substitute inputs or products when cheaper/more valuable; use limited resources where the last unit returns most; compare time-different options by present value; test several price/yield levels for risk. Cost-cutting tips: know and update your cost per cow and per cwt weaned; check whether a cost cut loses more revenue than it saves; budget and market for a full-cost profit including owner labor and overhead; sell unneeded machinery; review feed, grazing, vehicles, insurance, depreciation, overhead; get managerial (accrual) financial statements, not just tax returns; if you pay no income tax your business is probably not profitable. Definitions: percent calf crop, replacement rate, death rate, cows per bull, animal unit (UNL: weight/1,000; weaned calves 0.65 AU, cow with calf 1.4 AU, mature bull 1.7 AU, horse 1.5 AU).

chunks.t: C1. Cow-Calf Herd Budget Decision Aid User's Manual (J. McGrann, 2017)
chunks.x: profitable. Definitions: percent calf crop, replacement rate, death rate, cows per bull, animal unit (UNL: weight/1,000; weaned calves 0.65 AU, cow with calf 1.4 AU, mature bull 1.7 AU, horse 1.5 AU).

chunks.t: C2. Herd Bull Investment - Annual Bull Cost Analysis (J. McGrann, 2019)
chunks.x: Calculates the annual cost of an owned herd bull, the economics of leasing bulls, and owning versus leasing with a calf buy-back premium. A bull is an investment paid out over 3-5 years. Ownership costs = depreciation (purchase price minus salvage/cull value, divided by years of use) + death loss + interest on the investment; operating costs = grazing, feed, health including the annual breeding soundness exam (BSE). Express cost per cow serviced, per calf and per cwt of calf weaned per cow exposed, and compute how much extra weaning weight would pay for a higher-priced bull. Cost per cow is very sensitive to the number of cows each bull services, which is why BSE, bull nutrition and management matter. A pricier bull that sires more marketable, heavier calves is not that costly per calf; but price alone does not guarantee genetic performance.

chunks.t: C3. Breeding Soundness Exam (BSE) Economics and Herd Bull Investment (McGrann & Richardson DVM, 2019)
chunks.x: The BSE is one of the most cost-effective cow-calf practices, because weaning percent on exposed females is the most important performance measure and it depends on fertile bulls. Risks of sub-fertile bulls: a small herd can lose a calf crop; big herds end up short of bulls; females cycle without conceiving, so calves are born later and wean lighter even with a long breeding season. The aid compares the revenue benefit of a BSE (more calves, earlier calves valued with a price slide, possibly fewer bulls needed) with its cost per exposed female, as a benefit-cost ratio. BSE cost includes vet, lab, supplies and owner time. Also covers annual herd bull investment cost as in C2.

chunks.t: B8. Beef Cow Herd Replacement Requirements Calculator (J. McGrann, 2021)
chunks.x: How many replacement females must enter the herd each year, and how many heifers must be exposed to produce them? Inputs: expected calvings per cow lifetime (longevity), age of replacements entering, culling rate, and losses other than age (culling open cows raises replacement needs). Then adjusts from weaned heifer selection to a heifer calving a live calf for death losses, culling and breeding results. Compares conventional AI + cleanup bulls with sexed-semen AI (sexed semen reduces the number of exposed females needed); natural service gives results similar to conventional AI + cleanup.

chunks.t: B4e. Replacement Females Marketing Alternatives and Auction Cost Calculator (J. McGrann, 2019)
chunks.x: Options: on-ranch direct sales (buyer pays freight; long-term contracts; "weekender" buyers; more time and advertising), internet with ranch pickup, video/online special sales, and auction special replacement sales (big buyer pool, secure payment; commission and freight are the main costs). Auction invoice costs: commission, yardage, insurance, brand inspection, chute charge, pregnancy test (avoid by testing before shipping), beef checkoff; plus owner hauling. Have full documentation (genetics, sire, source/age, breeding and health protocols, vet and AI service, projected calving dates) so any market is open. 96% of cow-calf operations have under 200 cows, so the replacement market is large. The buy price of heifers largely decides profit in heifer development ("profit is often purchased").

chunks.t: B4d. Allocation of Indirect Costs and Total Unit Cost (J. McGrann, 2015/2018)
chunks.x: With several enterprises, indirect costs (overhead) must be allocated to get each enterprise's TUC. Use a QuickBooks class for indirect and G&A costs (car/truck, fuel, benefits, hired labor and management, rents/leases, repairs by vehicles/machinery/buildings, non-income taxes, owner withdrawals for labor/management, conservation, insurance, utilities, professional fees, office, admin wages). Allocate by a logical, consistent rule: percent of management time, per acre for crops, or per head-day for cattle. Direct costs go away when the activity stops (feed, yardage, vet, breeding, purchased feeders; seed, fertilizer, chemicals, irrigation, crop insurance). Indirect costs continue regardless of volume (depreciation, repairs, labor and management, property tax, G&A). IRS depreciation (Section 179, zero salvage) is a poor measure of real depreciation; ask the CPA for "book depreciation" with realistic lives and salvage values. Finance cost = cash interest paid; for economic analysis use an opportunity-cost interest (cow-calf: half of operating cost x rate). TUC = direct + indirect (incl. G&A and owner management) + finance; when complete it ties to the business P&L. Yardage = indirect costs charged per head-day.

chunks.t: B4c. Replacement Heifer Inventory - Head Day and AUM Calculator (J. McGrann, 2018/2022)
chunks.x: Monthly reconciled heifer inventory by category and class (exposed, open, pregnant, calved; bulls too). Inventory equation: Ending = Total In - Total Out; In = beginning + purchases + transfers in + category changes in + births + longs; Out = sales + transfers out + category changes out + consumed + deaths + shorts. Shorts = missing at count; longs = extra cattle that can't be explained; if shorts exceed longs, suspect count errors or losses. Keep purchased cattle for resale separate from breeding stock for IRS (purchased breeding stock is on the depreciation schedule; book value = cost minus accumulated depreciation). Head-days (average of beginning and ending monthly inventory) are a good base for allocating fixed costs. AUM: a 1,000 lb animal = 1 AU; one AUM is about 780 lb of air-dry forage per month; e.g. 1,200 lb cow + 300 lb calf = 1.5 AU. AUMs support stocking-rate monitoring and grazing lease pricing.

chunks.t: C.5 Cattle and Horse Beginning/Ending Fiscal Year Inventory by Category (J. McGrann, 2022)
chunks.x: Records head and value per head of breeding cattle (cows, replacement heifers, bulls), market cattle (weaned, stocker, feeder, background, finishing) and horses at the start and end of the fiscal year, for the accrual-adjusted income statement and balance sheet. Footnote the valuation method: market value for management, cost minus depreciation for purchased breeding stock (IRS). Keep purchased breeding stock separate from raised stock and raised calves; separate raised vs purchased-for-resale market cattle. Suggested sales subaccounts: raised cattle sales (weaned, stocker/feeder, finished; always separate steers and heifers), breeding cattle purchases (bulls, cows, replacement heifers), raised breeding cattle sales (cull bulls, cows, heifers), purchased-for-resale sales (bred heifers, open culls, bred cows, pairs) matched against purchase cost. Always record net sales after all marketing costs; tag bulls at minimum.
